title: An Indian-Origin Founder Just Raised $8.5 Million to Replace the Back Offices That Employ Millions of Indians
excerpt: Champ AI, built by ex-Instacart engineers led by Jagannath Putrevu, wants AI agents to do the work that India's BPO industry has done for two decades. The irony is not lost on anyone.
body:
In the taxonomy of Silicon Valley startup pitches, few are as bracing as the one Jagannath Putrevu is making. The Indian-origin CEO of Champ AI, a startup that emerged from stealth last week with $8.5 million in seed funding, wants to build AI agents that can perform the back-office work — fixing orders, updating records, investigating fraud, filling out forms, placing phone calls — that companies currently outsource to human teams. Many of those human teams sit in India.

The funding round, led by Redpoint Ventures with participation from Defy.vc and SV Angel, also drew an angel investment from Max Mullen, an Instacart co-founder. Putrevu and his co-founders, Ted Cheng and Peter Lin, all previously worked at Instacart, where they saw first-hand how scaling a logistics business means drowning in operational busywork.

"We learned that as companies grow, the back office doesn't scale with them," Putrevu told reporters. "You end up with people jumping between documents, internal systems, forms, and phone calls. We're building agents that can do that work end to end."

## How It Works

Champ AI's product takes a company's internal policies and translates them into automated workflows that AI agents can execute. The agents can log into websites, navigate user interfaces, download documents, fill out spreadsheets, send emails, and even make phone calls. The system combines large language models — for understanding and reasoning about policies — with UI automation, allowing it to operate across enterprise software without requiring deep integrations.

The company claims more than ten paying customers across logistics, healthcare, and e-commerce. Arena Club, a sports-card marketplace, reported that Champ AI sped up its card-processing work by 30 percent. The platform promises deployment in weeks rather than the months typically required to onboard outsourced operations teams.

Putrevu is careful to position the technology as augmentation rather than wholesale replacement. "Companies still need people to own processes, monitor agent performance, and manage how these automated systems behave," he said. But the economic logic is unmistakable: if an AI agent can process orders, handle customer queries, and manage compliance checks at a fraction of the cost of a human team, the business case for outsourcing to lower-wage geographies weakens.

## The BPO Question

This is where the story becomes uncomfortable for anyone who cares about the Indian economy. India's IT services and business process outsourcing sector employs roughly five million people directly and supports an estimated 15 million more in ancillary roles. Companies like Infosys, Wipro, TCS, and Genpact built their empires on precisely the kind of rule-driven, repetitive, back-office work that Champ AI is automating.

The sector generated approximately $250 billion in revenue in 2025, making it one of India's largest sources of foreign exchange — and one of the primary economic engines that enabled the middle-class expansion of the past two decades. For the diaspora, the BPO boom was foundational: it funded education, enabled emigration, and created the professional class from which many NRI families emerged.

Champ AI is not alone in targeting this work. UiPath, Automation Anywhere, and Microsoft Power Automate have been chipping away at process automation for years. But the new wave of AI-agent startups — armed with large language models that can understand context, reason about exceptions, and learn from feedback — threatens to compress a transition that the industry expected to unfold over a decade into something far more abrupt.

NASSCOM, the Indian IT industry body, has been sounding cautiously optimistic notes about AI, arguing that the technology will create new categories of work even as it eliminates old ones. But the specifics of that optimism remain vague. When pressed, industry leaders tend to invoke "reskilling" and "moving up the value chain" — phrases that have been doing heavy lifting in Indian economic discourse for rather longer than their results would justify.

## The Diaspora Irony

There is a particular poignancy in the fact that Champ AI's CEO is of Indian origin. The Indian-American tech community has been among the most successful immigrant groups in Silicon Valley history — Sundar Pichai at Alphabet, Satya Nadella at Microsoft, Arvind Krishna at IBM. Their success was built on the same educational infrastructure and professional pipeline that feeds India's IT services sector.

Now, a new generation of Indian-origin founders is building the technology that could disrupt the very industry that made their success possible. It is not hypocrisy — technology does not respect origin stories — but it is a tension that the diaspora will increasingly have to reckon with.

For Indian-origin professionals in the US, the rise of AI agents also raises questions closer to home. H-1B visa holders working in enterprise software, quality assurance, and operations management — roles that overlap significantly with Champ AI's target use cases — face the same automation pressures as their counterparts in Bangalore and Hyderabad.

## What Comes Next

Champ AI is a six-person startup with $8.5 million. It is not going to dismantle India's BPO sector overnight. But it represents something larger: the acceleration of a trend that was already visible before generative AI arrived and has since become impossible to ignore.

The companies that will thrive — in India and in the diaspora — are those that move fastest to integrate AI into their operations rather than compete against it. For India's IT giants, that means investing aggressively in AI capabilities, even at the cost of cannibalising their own labour-intensive business models. For the diaspora, it means recognising that the economic foundations of the communities they came from are shifting beneath their feet.

Putrevu, for his part, sees the transition as inevitable. "The question isn't whether this work gets automated," he said. "It's whether companies do it with tools that are fast, reliable, and keep them in control — or whether they just wait until someone else does it for them."

The Indian economy has navigated technological disruption before. It can do so again. But the window for comfortable adaptation is narrowing, and $8.5 million seed rounds are the tremors before the earthquake.
nri_angle: Champ AI's Indian-origin CEO is building technology that directly threatens India's $250 billion IT services and BPO sector — the industry that transformed the Indian middle class and funded a generation of diaspora ambitions. The tension between Silicon Valley innovation and Bangalore employment is becoming impossible to ignore.
author: Diaspora Desk
